quick.summary: Why fixing code for your junior engineer hurts them, and how to guide instead.
quick.takeaway: Ask questions to narrow the focus until they find the answer themselves.

parts.title: Lead by asking

beats.line: My junior engineer was stuck. I typed the fix myself. Is that bad?
Think of a driving instructor. They sit in the passenger seat.
They do not grab the steering wheel at every single bump.
Because if they did, you would never learn how to drive.
Right. When you type the fix, you are grabbing the wheel.
You fix the code today, but you create a dependent engineer tomorrow.
I know. But fixing it takes ten seconds. Explaining takes twenty minutes.
That twenty minutes is an investment in your own future free time.
Okay. But how do I guide them without giving away the answer?

parts.cliff: How to ask questions that unlock the fix.

beats.line: Instead of telling them what is wrong, ask them where to look.
Ask them what part of the code failed first.
What if they still do not see the mistake?
Narrow the focus. Ask what a specific line of code is doing.
We call this technique guided discovery.
That sounds like a museum tour. Can I just say leading by asking?
I love that. Lead by asking.
Keep making the space smaller until they spot the bug themselves.
So I ask them to read the error log to me out loud.
Yes. Let them find the light switch themselves.

quiz.question: Your junior engineer is stuck on a broken query. What is your best first move?
options: Ask them which table they think is causing the error.
Take over their keyboard and fix the join.
Tell them the exact line number where they made a mistake.
Tell them to come back when they figure it out.
quiz.explanation: Guiding by asking narrows their focus without giving them the answer immediately.

quiz.question: Coaching someone to find the fix takes longer today but saves you time next month.
quiz.explanation: Coaching your team builds their independence, freeing you up from making basic fixes later.
